blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Statement forensics, lesson 9: Share count: buybacks, dilution, and stock-based compensation.

Here is the number that fools people every quarter: earnings per share went up, and nobody checks whether that happened because the business improved or because the share count shrank.

Buybacks reduce shares outstanding. Fewer shares, same net income, higher earnings per share. That looks like progress on a chart. But it is not growth, it is arithmetic.

Take a real pattern you can pull on Thomson ONE right now. Look at the five year share count history under the equity or capitalization tab. A company with flat net income and a share count dropping three percent a year will show earnings per share rising roughly three percent a year, compounding, with zero operating improvement. Now check the cash flow statement, financing section, for "repurchase of common stock." If that number is funded by debt issuance in the same period, you are watching leverage dressed up as shareholder return.

Now the other side: dilution. Stock based compensation gets expensed on the income statement, so it already hits earnings. But it also creates new shares over time, usually faster than the buyback retires them, especially at technology and biotech names. Check the diluted share count against the basic share count on the income statement. A widening gap between those two lines tells you dilution is running ahead of repurchases, even while the company announces a buyback program in its press releases.

The one mistake: people look at the buyback announcement dollar figure, like "two billion dollar authorization," and treat it as fact. An authorization is a ceiling, not a commitment. Check actual repurchases executed, in the cash flow statement, against shares actually retired, in the share count footnote. Companies routinely authorize more than they spend, and spend enough just to offset stock based compensation dilution, so the net share count barely moves even as headlines claim a buyback program.

What this reveals: whether reported earnings per share growth is real operating performance or financial engineering. What it cannot tell you: whether the capital would have earned a better return reinvested in the business, paying down debt, or returned as a dividend instead. That judgment sits with the capital allocation discipline shown over multiple years, not one quarter's authorization headline.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 42: Home buying and mortgages: stress test, amortization, and the numbers that matter.

Here's the number that trips up almost every client who hasn't bought in a while. The mortgage stress test, formally called the minimum qualifying rate, requires borrowers to qualify at whichever is higher: their contract rate plus two percentage points, or 5.25 percent. That floor has been in place since 2021 and hasn't moved for 2026. So if a lender offers your client 4.4 percent on a five year fixed, they still need to qualify at 6.4 percent, because 4.4 plus 2 beats the 5.25 floor.

Here's the worked example. A couple earning a combined 160,000 dollars a year wants to buy a 750,000 dollar home in Winnipeg with 20 percent down, so a 600,000 dollar mortgage. At their actual contract rate of 4.4 percent, amortized over 25 years, their payment is roughly 3,290 dollars a month. But the bank doesn't use that number to qualify them. It uses 6.4 percent, which pushes the qualifying payment to about 4,030 dollars a month. Their gross debt service ratio and total debt service ratio get calculated against that higher figure, not the real one. This is why clients get pre-approved for less than they expect, and why the actual payment they'll make feels comfortable by comparison.

On amortization: 25 years is still the max for insured mortgages, those with less than 20 percent down, under 2026 rules. For uninsured mortgages, 20 percent or more down, lenders can go to 30 years, and since August 2024 that 30 year option was also extended to first time buyers purchasing new builds with insured mortgages.

The one mistake I see constantly: advisors and buyers both use the contract rate to estimate borrowing power instead of the stress test rate. That overstates what a client can actually qualify for, sometimes by six figures on the purchase price, and it blows up financing conditions in the offer stage.

Communication, lesson 42: Questions that open: the difference between a good question and an interrogation.

Edgar Schein, the organizational psychologist who coined the term "humble inquiry," ran a thought experiment that's stuck with researchers for decades. He compared two ways a doctor can open a consultation. One: "What symptoms are you having?" The other: "Tell me what's been going on." Same intent, completely different physiology in the room. The first puts the patient in a witness box. The second hands them the pen.

That's the whole distinction you need today. A good question is open-ended and curiosity-first. An interrogation is closed-ended and verdict-first, even when it's phrased politely.

Here's the worked example. A prospective client tells you their portfolio dropped 18% last year against a benchmark that dropped 12%. Interrogation version: "Why didn't you rebalance in March?" That's a question with the answer already baked in, it's an accusation wearing a question mark. Opening version: "Walk me through what you were thinking in March when things started moving." Same facts, same 18% and 12%, but now the client is narrating instead of defending. Schein's research, and later work by Harvard's Alison Wood Brooks on conversational receptiveness, both found the same pattern: people share roughly twice as much substantive information when the question doesn't contain a hidden judgment.

The one mistake people make: stacking questions. You ask an open question, then before they finish, you add two more, narrowing it. "What happened in March, was it the advisor, did you panic?" That's not inquiry, that's cross-examination with extra steps. One question, then silence, then you let them fill it.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pull one company's five year basic and diluted share count from Thomson ONE, calculate the annual percent change in each, and note whether buybacks are outpacing or losing to stock based compensation dilution.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull one client's current mortgage pre-approval letter and recalculate their qualifying payment manually using the greater of contract rate plus 2 or 5.25 percent, then compare it to what the lender actually used.

Communication: Before your next client call, write down the first question you planned to ask. Rewrite it by removing any word that implies blame or a right answer, and check whether it could be answered in one sentence or requires a story.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Huang's Return Sparks Rally; Quebecor-Telus Talks Heat Up
blocks.script:
Nvidia leads everything today. Jensen Huang is back as chief executive, reinstated eleven days after resigning amid an affair scandal involving a woman with alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. The Globe and the BBC both report Nvidia's board acted under pressure from Donald Trump, and shares jumped as much as thirty seven per cent Monday, adding close to a trillion dollars in value and lifting the Nasdaq six and a half per cent, its best day since 2000. Tailwind: chip demand remains immense per recent earnings. Headwind: the board bypassed senior management and investigations continue. An evidence-based advisor says do not chase a one day pop, the stock's valuation already prices in a lot of optimism.

Quebecor and Telus are circling each other after Pierre Karl Péladeau and Victor Dodig met in Ottawa Monday to discuss Quebecor's thirty one billion dollar bid for Telus. Telus has gained about twenty four per cent since the offer surfaced while Quebecor has fallen roughly twenty per cent, shrinking the premium to near eleven per cent. Tailwind for Quebecor: Ottawa seems open to a three player telecom sector. Headwind: regulatory scrutiny and a narrowing offer. An advisor says don't trade merger arbitrage on headlines, deal risk here is still wide open.

Wealthsimple's Michael Katchen is Report on Business magazine's Innovator of the Year, built a low cost platform chasing bank customers. The tailwind is scale and brand trust with younger investors. The headwind is thinning fee margins as competitors cut prices too. An advisor says low cost platforms are good for simple portfolios, but still check what you're actually invested in.

Celestica's Rob Mionis is named Strategist of the Year for turning the contract manufacturer into a key supplier for artificial intelligence hyperscalers, driving a huge stock run. Tailwind: data centre demand. Headwind: concentration risk if hyperscaler spending slows. An advisor says a single theme stock needs sizing discipline, not conviction alone.

Cineplex's Ellis Jacob takes Corporate Citizen of the Year honours for steering the chain through a near collapse. Tailwind: moviegoing has stabilized. Headwind: streaming still pressures ticket volumes long term. An advisor says cyclical consumer names like this belong in small positions, not core holdings.

blocks.title: Brackets, BCSC Ban, and HNW Private-Market Push
blocks.script:
Start with the tax numbers you'll use in client meetings this week. The 2026 federal brackets are out: 14 per cent on the first 58,523 dollars, then 20.5, 26, 29, and 33 per cent above 258,482 dollars. That 14 per cent bottom rate is down from 15, and this is the first full year it applies, after a mid-2025 blended rate. For incorporated clients pulling salary versus dividends, rerun the numbers now, the bracket shift changes the optimal split for 2026 remuneration planning. Also on the calendar: the final Alberta Child and Family Benefit payment of the year lands Friday, worth flagging if you have Alberta clients doing year-end benefit clawback planning.

Regulatory note. The British Columbia Securities Commission has banned a woman for life over a US 144-million-dollar penny stock scheme, a reciprocal order stripping her of registrant, adviser, and director registrations after a US jury verdict. It's a reminder for CIRO-registered advisors here that cross-border enforcement actions do follow people into Canadian registration.

Bigger structural story for your HNW book: private markets firms, the big US alternative managers, are pivoting hard at high-net-worth individuals, and Canadian advisors are already in the crosshairs, per Wealth Professional. CAZ Investments has entered Canada partnering with iCapital to build private-market vehicles for advisors here. If you've got clients asking about private credit or private equity sleeves, expect more inbound pitches and more product on bank platforms soon, Manulife is also rolling out longevity-focused advisor training this week, aimed at caregiving and longevity conversations, which pairs well with any HNW retirement or transition discussion.

Estate planning update that matters for blended families or clients using assisted reproduction: an Ontario appeal court reversed a lower decision and ruled a sperm-donor-conceived child is entitled to inherit, overturning the original parentage finding. If you have clients with donor-conceived children or non-traditional family structures, their wills need review, this ruling signals courts will look past formal parentage categories.

Dimensional Fund Advisors, Scotia Wealth, Manitoba Hydro, United Way Winnipeg, the Jets, and the Bombers: nothing new from any of them today.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Wildfire Report, Scams, Silica, and a Strike Vote
blocks.script:
Start with the wildfire report. The Manitoba government released its final review of the 2025 wildfire response today, and it does not pull punches: the province says crews faced equipment shortages and staff fatigue during what became a record-breaking fire season, and it recommends more money, staff and equipment before next year. For clients with cottage or rural property in the burn zones, this is the document insurers and municipalities will be referencing all winter.

On the back of that fire season, there's a fraud story worth repeating to anyone buying real estate right now. A Flin Flon woman who lost her home in the wildfires was trying to buy a replacement when scammers hacked into email communications tied to her lawyer and redirected her closing funds. She's out more than 170 thousand dollars, per CBC. This is now five Manitobans hit by the same lawyer-impersonation scheme in two months. If you've got a closing coming up, confirm wire instructions by phone, not email, every single time.

On crime policy, the province is adding 12 new police officers aimed at retail theft, four in Brandon and eight joining RCMP investigations in rural communities. Expect this to come up with any client running a retail or hospitality business outside the Perimeter.

Up north, University College of the North staff voted overwhelmingly to reject the school's final wage offer of two percent a year and now have a strike mandate. The union says that leaves workers falling behind counterparts at Red River College Polytechnic. Watch for a strike notice in the coming weeks, it would hit Thompson and The Pas hardest.

blocks.script: If you train for long distances, pay attention to this one. Outside reported today on a growing body of cardiology research into endurance athletes and heart risk. The pattern researchers keep finding is a J shaped curve: moderate exercise lowers your risk of atrial fibrillation, but very high volumes raise it. One widely cited meta-analysis found endurance athletes have close to four times the atrial fibrillation risk of non athletes, and a Swedish study of cross country skiers found thirty percent higher risk among those who raced more often. The flip side matters too: endurance athletes still show lower overall mortality and fewer strokes than sedentary people. For anyone doing serious volume, cardiologists quoted in the piece suggest periodic screening rather than cutting back blindly.

blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Macro & rates, lesson 9: Fiscal policy: deficits, debt to GDP, and how bond markets react.

The federal government tabled a budget last fall projecting a deficit near 42 billion dollars for fiscal year 2024 to 2025, and the parliamentary budget officer has flagged slippage above that since. Here's what you actually need to know: the deficit number alone tells you almost nothing. What moves bond markets is the trajectory of debt relative to the size of the economy, because that ratio tells lenders whether the debt is growing faster than the country's capacity to service it.

Take the federal debt to GDP ratio. Canada sits around 42 percent on a net basis, which sounds manageable next to the United States near 120 percent. But the bond market doesn't grade on a curve against other countries in isolation. It watches direction. If the ratio is falling, as it did through the 2000s, yields can stay calm even with deficits, because lenders see the numerator growing slower than the denominator. If the ratio is rising while growth slows, that's when you see term premium creep into long bonds. The 10 year Government of Canada yield carries a few basis points of extra compensation for that risk, on top of what short term rate expectations alone would justify.

The mistake people make is treating the deficit headline as the signal. A big one time deficit during a recession, fully offset by stronger growth after, is not the same risk as a smaller but structural deficit baked into the budget every year regardless of the cycle. The market prices the second kind differently, because it implies the debt ratio won't self correct. Thomson ONE carries the debt to GDP series and the budget balance history under the government finance statistics within the Canada economic database, worth pulling both together rather than the deficit figure alone.

Evidence based view: fiscal data tells you about solvency risk and the term premium embedded in long government yields. It does not tell you when a market reprices that risk, and it says nothing about currency or equity valuations on its own. Use it to question the plan's sensitivity to rate assumptions, not to time a trade.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 41: Alternative minimum tax: who it catches after the recent changes.

Starting with your incorporated owners and your physicians, the 2024 alternative minimum tax overhaul is still catching people off guard, and 2026 is the second full tax year it applies.

Here is the mechanism. Alternative minimum tax, or AMT, is a parallel tax calculation that strips out a lot of preferential treatment and applies a flat rate instead. For 2026, the AMT rate is 20.5 percent federally, up from 15 percent before the change. The exemption, the amount of income before AMT even kicks in, is now indexed and sits at roughly 177,000 dollars for 2026, up from the old flat 40,000 dollar exemption.

What changed that actually bites: only 50 percent of most donation tax credits now count against AMT, down from 100 percent. Capital gains inclusion for AMT purposes went from 80 percent to 100 percent. And employee stock option benefits, a big one for medical professionals and executives with equity comp, are now fully included instead of partially.

Worked example. A doctor incorporated through a medical professional corporation realizes a 300,000 dollar capital gain selling an investment property personally, and also donates 50,000 dollars of appreciated securities the same year. Under the old AMT rules this combination rarely triggered anything. Under 2026 rules, with full capital gains inclusion and only half the donation credit counting, her AMT liability can exceed her regular tax, meaning she pays the higher AMT amount. She does get that paid as a credit carried forward up to seven years, usable against regular tax in a future year, but the cash has to show up this year.

The one mistake: people plan large capital gains or large donations in isolation, checking only regular tax rules, and never run the AMT parallel calculation before year end. By the time their accountant catches it in April, the cash is already spent or the carry forward is wasted sitting unused for years because future income never gets high enough to absorb it.

For today, pull one client file who is planning either a large capital gain disposition or a large securities donation before December 31, and ask your tax preparer for an AMT estimate on that specific transaction before it closes.

Communication, lesson 41: Active listening: the three behaviours that clients actually notice.

Harvard Business Review ran a study years back asking people to name the manager who listened best to them. The answers didn't mention nodding, eye contact, or silence. They named three things: the person asked a question that built on what was just said, the person summarized back something specific, and the person didn't jump in with their own story.

You've probably been taught the textbook version of active listening. Lean forward, make eye contact, nod occasionally. That's stagecraft. Clients don't score you on posture. They score you on whether you proved you tracked the actual content.

Here's the worked example. A board member tells you the nonprofit's biggest donor just pulled a 40,000 dollar pledge for 2026 because of a staffing complaint. Weak response: "That's tough, these things happen." Strong response: "So the 40,000 dollar gap, is that about this year's budget or does it put the 2027 campaign at risk too." That single question tells her you did arithmetic on what she said and you're thinking one step ahead with her, not just absorbing.

The one mistake almost everyone makes is called conversational narcissism, a term from sociologist Charles Derber's 1979 study. The shift response. Someone shares a problem, you respond with your own similar story. "A donor pulled funding." "Oh, same thing happened to me in 2019." It feels like empathy. It's actually a topic hijack. Derber found it dominates most casual conversation, and it's deadly in advisory work because it makes the client the supporting character in your anecdote.

Your practice task today: in your next real conversation, whether a client call or a board meeting, catch yourself the first time you feel the urge to say "that reminds me" or "same thing happened to me." Don't say it. Ask a follow-up question about their situation instead.

lessons.task: In your next real conversation, notice the first urge to redirect to your own story, and replace it with one specific follow-up question about theirs.
lessons.drill: Record one five-minute conversation (with consent) or a mock client call. Afterward, count: number of times you summarized specifics back (names, numbers, dates mentioned), and number of times you redirected to your own story. blocks.title: Macklem's Exit Leads a Week of Corporate Shake-ups
blocks.script:
Tiff Macklem is on the watch list through the Bank of Canada, and he leads today because his departure reshapes the biggest file in Canadian finance. The Bank of Canada governor confirmed he will not seek a second term, with his mandate ending June 2, 2027. The Globe's business brief flags this as one of five files to watch this week. The tailwind is a clean, orderly transition with a search committee already working. The headwind is months of speculation that could unsettle rate expectations. An evidence-based advisor would say: don't trade around a governor change, your mortgage and portfolio plan shouldn't hinge on who holds the gavel.

Apiary Therapeutics is the UBC spinout built around stem-cell scientist Peter Zandstra, engineering white blood cells to act as drug-delivery machines. The company just raised seven point three million dollars, and the Globe reports investors are buzzing. The tailwind is Zandstra's track record and a genuinely novel platform. The headwind is that this is pre-revenue biotech, years from any product. An advisor would say: fine as a speculative sliver, never as a core holding.

Poundland is the UK discount retailer now days from collapse unless it finds a buyer, the BBC reports. It's the latest marker of British retail distress. The tailwind, if any, is private equity interest in a recognizable brand. The headwind is creditor pressure and a shrinking runway. An advisor would say: distressed retail is a trading story, not an investing one.

Compass Group, the world's largest catering company, is planning to shift its primary stock listing from London to New York. The move reflects its heavy North American revenue base. The tailwind is deeper US liquidity and valuation. The headwind is another blow to London markets and UK pension exposure. An advisor would say: listing venue rarely changes the underlying business, don't chase the headline.

blocks.title: Estate Rulings and Advisor Training Shape Today's Practice
blocks.script:
Start with the estate case, because it changes how you talk to clients about wills. The Ontario Court of Appeal has overturned a lower court ruling in the estate of a man named Jake Edmonstone, who was conceived through an anonymous sperm donor during his mother's common-law relationship. The amendments include clauses stating that when a parent conceives a child via assisted reproduction and has a spouse at the time of conception, that spouse will legally be considered one of the child's parents. The lower court had placed the burden of proof on the child and his mother to show the deceased consented to parenthood. The appeal court found that was backwards, and that the onus shouldn't have been on them to prove consent before conception. This is your cue for incorporated professionals and blended families without wills: intestacy outcomes on assisted reproduction are not settled law, they're being written case by case.

Paired with that, the Globe and Mail has useful guidance for anyone whose spouse handled the household finances and has died. The core advice: don't make irreversible decisions while grieving, get organized first, locate accounts, beneficiary designations, and the will, before touching investments. That's a script you can lift directly for widowed clients this week.

On the practice side, Manulife is rolling out a longevity training program for advisors. It's meant to help advisors have broader conversations with clients about life in retirement, extending to housing, caregiving needs and social connections. The courses launch in English and French through Manulife's continuing education centre, with two modules opening December 11th and more planned for 2027. Worth booking if you deal with aging clients or adult children as caregivers.

blocks.script:
Start with the weather, because everyone in your office will be talking about it. Winnipeg saw its first real snowfall of the season on Sunday, November 22nd. The latest measurable snowfall on record for the city fell on November 22, 2016, exactly ten years ago, and Sunday's dusting tied that record. David Phillips, an emeritus climatologist with Environment Canada, called it one of the latest first snows Winnipeg has ever seen. Normally you'd be dealing with winter before Halloween.

On the policy side, a smaller story but worth flagging for clients who touch the justice system: the Manitoba government quietly phased out its fine option program, which lets people work off court fines they can't pay, then reinstated it last month after concerns were raised. It's a reminder that provincial program changes here can move fast and reverse just as fast.

Bell MTS confirmed a cyberattack this week. The telecom said in a statement that the attack resulted in customer email account lockouts and password resets, and compromised personal customer information in Manitoba. If you have clients on Bell MTS, expect questions about identity protection steps.

On healthcare, four Manitoba hospitals are now grey-listed by the Manitoba Nurses Union: Health Sciences Centre and St. Boniface Hospital in Winnipeg, plus Seven Oaks and Thompson General. The union says the "mark of disgrace" stays until its safety recommendations are acted on. That's a live question for board colleagues in the health sector: grey-listing doesn't close a department, but it signals staff won't apply there and existing nurses are being discouraged from taking shifts.

Mark Scheifele made Winnipeg Jets history Saturday night, and it still wasn't enough. Per CBC, Scheifele scored his 380th career goal to pass Dale Hawerchuk as the franchise's all-time leading goal scorer, and fans at Canada Life Centre gave him a long standing ovation. blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Evidence arsenal, lesson 10: Behavioural gap: investor returns versus fund returns.

Here is the number that should bother anyone who thinks picking a good fund is the whole job. Morningstar's annual "Mind the Gap" study has run this for years, and the gap sits consistently between 1.5 and 2 percentage points a year, the fund's own reported return minus what the average dollar actually earned in it. Not a small rounding error. Over a decade, compounded, that is the difference between a comfortable retirement and a tight one.

The mechanism is simple. Morningstar calculates fund returns time-weighted, meaning it assumes you put money in on day one and never touched it. But investors are dollar-weighted. They add money after a fund has run up, and they pull money out after it falls. So the fund's own math says 9 percent a year. The investors living inside that fund, averaged by how much money moved when, earned maybe 7 percent. Same fund, two different realities.

Take a concrete case. Suppose a fund returns 10 percent in year one, then drops 15 percent in year two, then returns 12 percent in year three. The fund's three-year annualized return is roughly 1.8 percent. But if most investor money poured in right after that strong year one, chasing the performance, and a chunk fled during the year-two drop, the dollar-weighted investor return comes in negative. The fund survived. The investor did not, not in return terms.

The one mistake is confusing a fund's track record with your own outcome. People read a five-star rating, assume that star rating is what they will personally earn, and ignore that the rating says nothing about entry and exit timing, theirs or anyone else's.

What this reveals: performance chasing has a real, measured cost, and it is bigger than most fee arguments. What it cannot tell you: whether any specific client behaved this way. You have to check that against their own statements, not the industry average.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 40: Attribution rules: spousal loans, the prescribed rate, and income splitting that works.

Here's the problem income splitting is designed to solve. One spouse sits in the top bracket, the other has almost no income. If the high earner just hands money to the low earner to invest, the Canada Revenue Agency attributes all the income and capital gains right back to the person who gave the money. The attribution rules exist specifically to stop that. Gifts don't work. Loans at zero or low interest don't work. There's exactly one structure that does: a loan at the prescribed rate, documented properly.

The prescribed rate is set quarterly by the CRA and it's been at 4 percent since the second quarter of 2024, holding steady through the fourth quarter of 2025. For the first quarter of 2026, confirm the published rate before you quote it, but assume 4 percent unless CRA has announced otherwise.

Here's the mechanic. The high-income spouse lends money to the low-income spouse, in writing, at the prescribed rate in effect the day the loan is made. That rate is locked in for the life of the loan, even if the prescribed rate rises later. The low-income spouse invests the funds and must actually pay the interest each year, by January 30 of the following year, every year, without missing one.

Worked example. Dr. Chen earns 380,000 dollars and sits in Manitoba's top bracket near 50.4 percent combined. Her spouse has no income. She lends 500,000 dollars at 4 percent. Interest owed is 20,000 dollars a year, which he pays her, and she reports as income, and he deducts as a carrying cost against his investment income. He invests the 500,000, earns say 6 percent, or 30,000 dollars. The first 20,000 is offset by the interest deduction, so only 10,000 dollars of investment income lands in his hands at his low bracket, instead of 30,000 taxed at hers.

The one mistake: missing the January 30 interest payment, even once. Miss it and the CRA attributes all income back to the lender retroactively for that year and every year after. There's no second chance on this one.

Communication, lesson 40: Your voice on the page: sounding like yourself in written content.

William Zinsser, who taught writing at Yale for years and wrote "On Writing Well," gave the clearest test I know for voice: read your draft out loud. If you wouldn't say it to a person sitting across from you, cut it. He built an entire career on one observation, that most bad writing comes from people trying to sound like someone else, usually someone more impressive.

Here's the worked example. You draft a LinkedIn post about a board meeting. First version: "Today's discussion yielded valuable insights regarding stakeholder engagement strategies moving forward." Twenty words, zero information, and nobody talks like that over coffee. Second version: "Today the board spent forty minutes on one question: why donors give once and don't come back. I didn't have a good answer. That bothered me." Twenty-six words, but it's specific, it admits something, and it sounds like a person, not a press release.

The mistake is almost always the same: writers reach for formal vocabulary because they think authority lives in bigger words. It doesn't. Authority lives in specificity and in the willingness to say something true that a committee wouldn't approve. You coach clients to be the hero of their own story. The same rule applies to you on the page. If every sentence could have been written by your competitor, you haven't written anything yet.

Here's the test that catches it fast. Take any sentence you've drafted and ask: would I say this exact sentence to a client at a dinner table. If the answer is no, that sentence is costume, not voice.

Here is the number that should bother anyone who thinks picking a good fund is the whole job. blocks.title: Loonie, Loblaw, and Ottawa's New Wingman Drone
blocks.script:
Start with the Bank of Canada, because it's on the watch list and it's everywhere in the feed. The central bank sets the interest rate that shapes your mortgage and your savings account. Right now it's in the news two ways: the Globe's weekly quiz asks who replaces Tiff Macklem as governor, and the loonie keeps sliding, now around 69.85 cents US as the Globe reports widening Canada-US rate gaps weigh on the currency. The tailwind is that a weaker loonie helps exporters. The headwind is pricier imports and leadership uncertainty clouding the policy outlook. An evidence-based advisor tells you not to bet a portfolio on who gets the governor's chair, build around what you control.

Loblaw is next. Canada's largest grocer, running Real Canadian Superstore, No Frills, and Shoppers Drug Mart. The Globe reports it's adding more discount banners after third-quarter same-store grocery sales came in flat, even as those discount banners grew. The tailwind is cost-conscious shoppers trading down into stores Loblaw already owns. The headwind is margin pressure and a flat top line signaling real consumer fatigue. An advisor says price it like any defensive retailer facing elastic demand, it's a steady holding, not a growth story.

Dominion Dynamics, the Ottawa defence firm building Canada's first autonomous wingman drone to fly beside crewed fighter jets. The Globe reports it's assembled a dozen-company consortium, aiming to finalize the design by March and have demonstrators flying by late 2028. The tailwind is Ottawa's defence spending appetite. The headwind is a young private company betting its future on government being its first customer, with a long timeline to revenue. An advisor calls this venture-stage defence tech, not core portfolio material.

Restaurant Brands International, parent of Burger King, Tim Hortons, and Popeyes. An Ontario Superior Court dismissed a lawsuit alleging franchisees bought unsafe chicken, with the Globe reporting the judge called it a diversion from a contract dispute. The tailwind is one less legal overhang. The headwind is that franchisee supply-chain friction hasn't actually gone away. An advisor says single-lawsuit outcomes rarely move a multi-brand franchisor's valuation, watch royalty growth instead.

blocks.title: Shilo Growth, PC Chaos, Tesla Fight, Crash Report
blocks.script:
Start with the number that matters most for southwestern Manitoba: nearly double. That is what CFB Shilo, the military base east of Brandon, is planning over the next decade, according to the CBC. The base commander, Lieutenant Colonel Jack Nguyen, told the Brandon Chamber of Commerce the base could add about 1,100 Canadian Armed Forces staff, growing the total to somewhere between 2,400 and 2,500 people. The Brandon mayor called it one of the largest investments in the city since the old Maple Leaf Foods plant went up almost 30 years ago. If you have clients with exposure to Westman real estate, construction, or retail, this is the kind of federal spending wave that shows up in local order books for years.

Closer to home, Manitoba's Progressive Conservatives are dealing with an embarrassing leak. The NDP obtained a draft Tory news release naming Konrad Narth as leader heading into the 2027 election, before the party's own executive council had even voted on the question, CBC reports. That lands the same week the government introduced new legislation toughening licensing rules for security guards, including mandatory de-escalation and cultural awareness training, brought forward by Justice Minister Matt Wiebe.

The PCs are also going after the NDP on the Tesla file, arguing the decision to pull Tesla Motors Canada out of the province's electric vehicle rebate program put public money at risk. Expect that argument to keep running in question period.

A federal investigation into last year's deadly plane crash at St. Theresa Point has raised concerns about weight balance and fuel storage on a flight that, per the report, almost didn't happen at all. Four people died.

In Winnipeg policing news, a man near the top of Canada's 25 most wanted list was arrested in the city, part of a reward program covering several remaining fugitives.

And in the north, Wasagamack First Nation says its operations are "in jeopardy" amid a legal fight over an attempt to oust its chief following a financial disclosure.

blocks.script:
COP31 is the biggest story for you this morning. With just two official days of talks left in Antalya, negotiators published a slimmed down draft that stripped out any reference to ending the use of fossil fuels compared to a first draft. Panama's environment minister has threatened to block any final text that lacks a clear fossil fuel transition path, and the Guardian is calling it a potential ghost COP. Amid that, young leaders from Germany, Argentina, Turkiye and Romania used the stage to push education and participation as an antidote to climate anxiety, a reminder your younger clients are watching this closely.

Closer to home, a genuinely newsy disclosure: Environment Canada officials told MPs this week that the decision to stop Environment Canada's work on banning exports of thermal coal came down from the political level, after years of work trying to enforce it through existing law. That's relevant if you've got clients in coal logistics or B.C. port infrastructure.

On the LNG file, Ottawa just handed Woodfibre LNG, near Squamish, a $200 million federal cash injection to support a nearly 25 per cent increase in capacity, while scientists and advocates still can't get the emissions modelling data behind its permit application.

blocks.title: Liver on Life Support, Aging Runners, and Fat-Burning Science
blocks.script:
Researchers in Australia kept a donated human liver alive outside the body for seven weeks, nearly triple the previous two-week record set in Switzerland, according to MIT Technology Review. It ran on an automated perfusion system feeding it blood and nutrients. Long term, this points toward repairing damaged organs before transplant, easing the shortage you hear about constantly.

On training, Outside reports a new study on master athletes found older runners burn more energy at the same pace, tied to weakened calf and Achilles function, with losses compounding as speed increases. The sample was small and only two treadmill speeds were tested, but the takeaway for anyone over forty still running or lifting is clear: prioritize calf raises and lower-leg strength work.

blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Industry structure, lesson 10: Railways and infrastructure: operating ratios and capital intensity.

Canadian National Railway reported an operating ratio of 61.6 percent for the third quarter of 2025. That single number tells you more about a railway than almost anything else on the income statement, so start there.

Operating ratio is operating expenses divided by revenue. A ratio of 61.6 percent means for every dollar of revenue, 61.6 cents went to running the railway: fuel, labor, equipment, track maintenance. The other 38.4 cents is operating income before interest and tax. Lower is better. This is the inverse of a margin, and that trips people up constantly. A falling operating ratio is improvement. A rising one is deterioration. Say it out loud when you read it, because the instinct to treat big numbers as good will mislead you here.

Now put it against capital intensity. Railways spend enormous sums maintaining track, bridges, and rolling stock just to keep the business standing still. CN's capital expenditure has run close to 19 to 20 percent of revenue in recent years, per its filings, which you can pull from Thomson ONE under the capital expenditure line in the cash flow statement, cross checked against the estimates tab for consensus capex as percent of sales. Compare that to a software company from an earlier lesson, where capex might be 3 or 4 percent of revenue. That gap is the entire story of why railways need decades to earn back an asset and why free cash flow lags net income so visibly in this sector.

The mistake people make is comparing operating ratios across industries, treating a utility's 70 percent ratio as worse than a railway's 62 percent. Different cost structures, different regulatory regimes, different asset lives. Operating ratio is a within-sector tool. It tells you whether CN is running tighter than Canadian Pacific Kansas City or than its own five-year average. It does not tell you whether a railway is a better business than an insurer or a REIT. That comparison needs the full financial plan, not one ratio borrowed from one chart of accounts.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 39: Charitable giving: donation credits, gifts of securities, and donor advised funds.

Here's the number that changes how you talk to incorporated business owners about giving. If you donate shares with an accrued capital gain directly to a registered charity, the capital gains inclusion rate on that donation drops to zero. Not fifty percent, zero. That rule has been in place federally for years now and it's still the single most underused move in Canadian philanthropy.

Here's the mechanics. Federally, donation credits work on a two tier system for 2025: fifteen percent on the first two hundred dollars donated, twenty nine percent above that, and in some cases thirty three percent on the portion that would otherwise be taxed at the top federal bracket. In Manitoba, the provincial credit is 10.8 percent on the first two hundred dollars and 17.4 percent above that. Combined, you're looking at roughly forty six percent credit on larger gifts.

Now the worked example. A client holds one hundred thousand dollars of public company shares, original cost base twenty thousand dollars. That's an eighty thousand dollar gain. Sell the shares first, then donate cash, and half that gain, forty thousand dollars, gets added to taxable income. Donate the shares directly instead, and the inclusion rate on that gain is zero. Nothing gets added. The client still gets a donation receipt for the full hundred thousand dollars, same as if they'd given cash. For someone in Manitoba's top bracket, avoiding tax on forty thousand dollars of gain saves roughly twenty thousand dollars, on top of the donation credit itself.

The one mistake people make: selling the shares first and then donating the cash proceeds. Once you sell, the gain is locked in and the zero inclusion rate doesn't apply. The shares have to transfer in kind, broker to charity, before any sale happens.

For incorporated owners with lumpy income, a donor advised fund lets them make the gift and get the receipt this year, then recommend grants to specific charities over following years. Useful when there's an unusual spike in corporate dividends or a sale event.

Communication, lesson 39: Apologizing well: ownership without self-abasement.

Business researcher Karen Cates at Northwestern's Kellogg School studied executive apologies and found something counterintuitive: the apologies that rebuilt trust fastest were short, specific, and didn't ask anyone to feel sorry for the apologizer. The ones that failed usually had one of two problems. Either no real ownership, just "mistakes were made." Or too much ownership, spiraling into self-flagellation that made the other person comfort the wronged party, which flips the whole transaction backward.

Here's the structure that works, four parts, roughly fifteen seconds spoken: name the specific action, name the specific impact, state what you're doing differently, stop talking.

Worked example. You're on a nonprofit board. You missed sending board materials 48 hours before the meeting, as your bylaws require, and two members showed up unprepared to vote on a $40,000 grant allocation. Bad version: "I'm so sorry, I've just been completely overwhelmed, I feel terrible, you have no idea how much pressure I'm under." That's 30 seconds about you. Good version: "I sent the board packet six hours before the meeting instead of 48. That meant two of you voted on the grant without time to review it. Starting next cycle, packets go out nine days before, with a calendar reminder I've already set." Fourteen seconds. No adjectives about your feelings. Done.

The one mistake: over-apologizing, which research from Maurice Schweitzer at Wharton on trust repair shows actually reduces perceived competence. Every extra "I'm just so sorry" after the facts are stated reads as either fishing for reassurance or padding time instead of fixing the problem. The listener starts managing your emotions instead of trusting your correction.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pull CN and CPKC's trailing twelve month operating ratios from Thomson ONE and note which one improved year over year and by how much.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull one client file with appreciated public securities and calculate the tax saved if they donated shares in kind versus cash, using their actual cost base and current bracket.
Communication: Write out, in the four-part structure, an apology for something small you actually did this week. Time yourself saying it out loud. If it runs past 20 seconds, cut adjectives first.

blocks.title: Anthropic's record IPO, Quebecor-Telus fight top Canada's business news
blocks.script:
Anthropic priced its initial public offering at 83 US dollars a share overnight, above its targeted range, raising 81 billion dollars. The BBC and CBC both call it the biggest stock market debut on record, valuing the Claude chatbot maker at 1.51 trillion dollars as it starts trading on Nasdaq today. Tailwind: investor demand ran roughly seven times oversubscribed. Headwind: a huge share count frees up fast, and BBC's Simon Jack asks if this pops the AI bubble. An evidence-based advisor says don't chase day-one IPO pops, you're buying hype before fundamentals.

Quebecor is in the news for its 31 billion dollar bid to buy Telus, and even Quebecor's own CEO has conceded the deal squeezes competition from four national players to three. BCE confirmed, per the Globe, it has held talks with Telus about a response, and Prime Minister Carney, at APEC, wouldn't say whether Ottawa can accept losing a major telecom player. Tailwind for Quebecor: a 60 percent premium gets attention. Headwind: regulatory hurdles look steep. An advisor says telecom consolidation plays are binary bets on Ottawa, size positions accordingly.

Telus sits at the center of that fight as the target, warning of serious concerns with the unsolicited offer. Tailwind: a takeover premium lifts the stock near term. Headwind: uncertainty drags on while the special committee reviews. An advisor tells clients not to hold shares purely on deal speculation.

BCE, Telus's rival and possible white knight, is weighing its own move after preliminary talks, the Globe reports. Tailwind: it could block a competitor from growing. Headwind: any BCE counter-bid adds debt to an already leveraged balance sheet. An advisor notes BCE's dividend yield is attractive but watch payout sustainability if a deal emerges.

Bank of Montreal says it has achieved quantum utility, the first Canadian bank to use quantum computing for practical work, the Globe reports. Tailwind: early mover status in a race among global banks. Headwind: practical payoff remains unproven at scale. An advisor says interesting research story, not yet an earnings driver.

Meta is in headlines because Loblaw will let Canadians shop using Meta's Muse AI assistant, the first Canadian retailer to partner directly, per the Globe. Tailwind: positions Meta's AI commerce push globally. Headwind: adoption and trust with shoppers is unproven. An advisor would note this is a small revenue test, not a thesis changer for Meta.

blocks.title: KPMG Breach, RRSP Reform, CIRO Enforcement Today
blocks.script:
Start with KPMG. The firm confirmed yesterday that a cybersecurity breach let an unauthorized party access client tax documents, and it's now contacting affected clients. KPMG hasn't disclosed how many clients, how many files, or how the attacker got in, but it says the data isn't showing up online or being misused. This fits a pattern: the Globe and Mail has reported that at least four major Bay Street law firms, McCarthy Tétrault, Davies Ward Phillips and Vineberg, Bennett Jones, and Borden Ladner Gervais, have had similar breaches. If you have clients who use KPMG for tax prep or corporate structuring, especially incorporated professionals and business owners, this is worth a proactive call. Ask whether their accountant has been in touch, and whether sensitive estate or corporate documents sat in that environment.

On regulation, CIRO, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, issued two notices yesterday. It's holding a settlement hearing for advisor Brady James Rak over gatekeeper obligation allegations, and it sanctioned Arthur Silber in a separate decision. Nothing earth-shaking, but worth knowing if either name surfaces with a client who's moved dealers recently.

The bigger planning story is still Budget 2026's RRSP-for-life proposal. Ottawa wants to merge RRSP, or Registered Retirement Savings Plan, and RRIF, or Registered Retirement Income Fund, rules so clients never have to formally convert at 71. But minimum withdrawals still start at 71, at the same 5.28 percent rate, rising with age. So this is paperwork relief, not a tax break. The one real change: a surviving spouse could become a successor holder more simply. Consultation runs to January 8th, so don't change anyone's retirement plan yet, but flag it to clients turning 71 soon so they don't panic about forced conversions.

blocks.title: Throne Speech, Tesla Ruling, and Siege on Siloam
blocks.script:
A Manitoba judge has ordered the Kinew government to explain, under oath, who decided to cut Tesla out of the province's EV rebate program and why. Court of King's Bench Justice Elissa Neville called it an "exceptional and unusual" remedy, giving the government ten days from November 13 to file a sworn affidavit, with Tesla's lawyers allowed to cross-examine whoever signs it. Tesla has been fighting this since the exclusion began in March 2025, arguing it cost buyers 560,000 dollars and that Premier Kinew's own comments about Elon Musk and tariffs point to a political motive, not a funding decision. The province still says the whole thing is a budget call and unreviewable by the courts. Watch this one, it could get awkward for the government in the legislature.

Speaking of the legislature, Tuesday's throne speech set the table for next year's election. The NDP promised a middle class tax cut starting in 2027, a white collar crime unit, more uniformed police in schools, and two emergency room reopenings including Victoria Hospital next summer. The province says that step down unit will run one nurse per patient. On the business side, Manitoba pledged to match Ottawa's new tax deduction for business and hired a chief mining officer to chase investment. Interim PC leader Konrad Narth called it short on substance.

Steinbach flood victims are getting two million dollars in provincial compensation, though only for one of the two years they were flooded out, in 2024 and 2025.

Winnipeg police have made race based use of force data collection mandatory department wide, a move the service frames as an accountability and transparency step.

blocks.script: Canada has officially lost its measles elimination status, CBC reports, a year after sustained transmission of the same virus strain since October 2024. The country had held that status since 1998. Samira Jeimy from Western University's Schulich School of Medicine says Canada lost its status because two-dose vaccine coverage dropped below the 95 percent threshold required to stop sustained transmission. If you're advising clients on benefits or group health plans, this is the kind of population-level risk that insurers watch. On training: a small new study covered by Outside Online compared 18 young runners, average age 26, against 18 master runners, average age 63. The gap in energy cost widened at the faster speed, from about five percent to about thirteen percent, though the study tested only two moderate speeds.

blocks.script: The Canadian Paediatric Society issued new guidance this month urging doctors to routinely ask teen patients about healthy relationships and dating violence. The society says one third of Canadian teens experience some form of physical, psychological, sexual, or technology-related abuse in relationships, including online tracking by a partner. For clients with teenagers, this is a cue to normalize that conversation at home too, not just in the doctor's office. On the financial side, Employment Insurance parental benefits for 2026 pay 55 percent of average insurable earnings, up to 729 dollars a week, for standard leave up to 40 shared weeks. Extended leave pays 33 percent, up to 437 dollars a week, over 69 shared weeks. The Canada Child Benefit for the current year runs up to 7,787 dollars annually per child under six, phasing out as household income rises.

Company & Economy Analysis, Valuation reps, lesson 9: Scenario valuation: bull, base, bear, and probability weighting.

A single discounted cash flow number is a lie dressed up as precision. You put in one growth rate, one margin assumption, one discount rate, and the model spits out a figure that looks exact to the penny. It never is. The honest fix is to build three cases and weight them by how likely you actually think they are.

Take a name like Canadian Natural Resources. In the base case, say you assume West Texas Intermediate averages 70 US dollars a barrel through the forecast window, production grows modestly, and you land on a fair value of 48 dollars a share. In the bull case, oil runs to 85, free cash flow jumps, and your value comes out near 62 dollars. In the bear case, oil slides to 55 on demand weakness, and your value drops to 34 dollars. Now assign probabilities. Not fifty-fifty-zero, that is lazy. Say 25 percent bull, 50 percent base, 25 percent bear. The weighted value is point two five times 62, plus point five times 48, plus point two five times 34. That is 15.5 plus 24 plus 8.5, which comes to 48 dollars. In this case the weighted figure lands close to your base case, which tells you the distribution is roughly symmetric. If the weighted number drifts far from the base case, that is the real signal, it means your downside or upside is doing more work than your gut assumed.

The one mistake people make is building three cases that only differ in the growth rate while holding margins and multiples fixed. That is not three scenarios, it is one scenario dressed three times. Bull and bear need their own margin assumptions and their own exit multiples, not just a faster top line.

This tells you the range of reasonable outcomes and where the market's current price sits inside that range. It cannot tell you which scenario will actually happen. That is still a judgment call, not a model output. Analysis first, technicals second, sector comparison third, same order as always.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 38: RRIF: minimum withdrawals, the age 65 pension credit, and the age of the younger spouse election.

Here is the thing most people over 71 get wrong about their RRIF, registered retirement income fund. They think the minimum withdrawal is fixed. It is not. It is a percentage of the December 31 balance from the prior year, and the percentage climbs every year you age.

For 2026, if the account holder is 71, the minimum factor is 5.28 percent. At 75, it jumps to 5.82 percent. At 80, it is 6.82 percent. At 90, it is 11.92 percent. These factors are set by the Income Tax Act and they do not change with interest rates, so say that to a client who thinks they are tied to bond yields. They are not.

Here is the worked example. A client turns 72 in 2026. Their RRIF held 500,000 dollars on December 31, 2025. The factor at age 72 is 5.40 percent. That means the 2026 minimum withdrawal is 27,000 dollars, and no tax is withheld at source on amounts up to the minimum. Over the minimum, withholding kicks in.

Now the age 65 pension credit. Once someone turns 65, RRIF withdrawals qualify as eligible pension income, which means up to 2,000 dollars of it is sheltered by the pension income credit federally, worth roughly 300 dollars in tax saved, and Manitoba has its own pension income amount on top of that on the provincial return. RRSP withdrawals do not qualify. This is one reason to convert part of an RRSP to a RRIF before age 71 if someone wants to use that credit earlier.

The one mistake: using the account holder's age for the minimum factor when the spouse is younger. You can elect, at the time the RRIF is set up, to base the minimum on the younger spouse's age instead. That election is made once, in writing, with the carrier, and it is irrevocable. A couple with a 70 year old RRIF holder and a 60 year old spouse can cut the minimum withdrawal nearly in half by electing the younger age, which matters a lot for income splitting and for deferring tax.

Communication, lesson 38: Humour: when it works in a professional setting and when it costs you.

Jennifer Aaker at Stanford ran the numbers on this. Her research with Naomi Bagdonas found that executives who use humour well are seen as 23 percent more competent and 25 percent more admired by their teams than those who don't, based on surveys across hundreds of leaders. That's a real, measurable business outcome, not a personality trait.

Here's the mechanism. Self-deprecating humour aimed at your own minor flaws signals confidence, because only someone secure enough can joke about their own slip. You open a board meeting with "I spent twenty minutes before this call trying to unmute myself, so if nothing else, I've lowered expectations early." That's three seconds, it's true, and it makes the room relax before you ask for something hard.

Now the version that costs you. Humour that punches at someone else in the room, even gently, even as a callback to an inside joke, creates an outgroup. A 2007 study by Robert Lynch and colleagues on humour styles found that "aggressive humour", jokes at another's expense, correlates with lower trust ratings from observers, even when the target laughs along. On a nonprofit board, where you're one of several voices and not the final decision maker, that's expensive. You're not the hero of that room, the cause is, and a joke that makes another board member the punchline undercuts the frame you're supposed to be holding for them.

The single mistake: timing it to the content instead of the room. People reach for a joke right when they're nervous, which is usually right before the ask or the hard number. That's the exact moment the room is listening hardest, and a joke there reads as deflection, not confidence.

Self-deprecating, early, about yourself only. Never aimed at a colleague, a client, or the room's mood. Never right before the ask.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Nvidia, Telus Lead A Pension-Heavy News Day
blocks.script:
Nvidia posted fiscal third quarter revenue guidance above Wall Street estimates, giving markets relief after a rout that had erased roughly two trillion dollars in value from its October peak. Shares rallied about four per cent after hours. The tailwind is that AI chip demand still looks healthy. The headwind is governance: the board confirmed on an investor call it will not rehire Jensen Huang despite his public openness to return. An evidence based advisor would say one earnings beat does not override a diversification plan.

Telus, the Vancouver based telecom Darren Entwistle built from a Western carrier into a national player, is now a takeover target as Quebecor pursues a bid. Prime Minister Carney, per the Globe, stayed mum on whether Ottawa would let the sector lose a national player, saying only that his government favours more competition. The tailwind is political pressure for a resolution. The headwind is prolonged uncertainty. An advisor would say event driven stocks need a sized position, not a bet.

L3Harris Technologies installed the router blamed for last week's nationwide ground stop, and the Federal Aviation Administration has now paused further installations while it investigates. The tailwind is a deep air traffic modernization contract pipeline. The headwind is Senate Democrats demanding answers before new work proceeds. An advisor would say single contractor headline risk rarely changes a long term thesis.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns router maker Juniper, says its equipment worked as configured when the outage hit seventeen of twenty two air traffic centres. The tailwind is HPE's networking business keeps winning critical infrastructure work. The headwind is reputational exposure even while disclaiming fault. An advisor would say wait for the root cause before reading much into the stock.

GE Vernova, the power equipment business spun off from General Electric, has formed an alliance to supply technology for the thirty billion dollar undersea NATO-L transmission line linking Canada and Europe. The tailwind is a multi decade grid buildout order book. The headwind is years of permitting risk before revenue lands. An advisor would say treat mega project headlines as thesis support, not a signal to trade.

OMERS has teamed with Transmission Developers Infrastructure to bid on an underwater electricity line from the Darlington nuclear plant into Toronto's Port Lands. The tailwind is regulated returns matching pension liabilities. The headwind is construction delays common to major transmission builds. An advisor would say this is exactly the patient capital role pension funds exist for.

La Caisse is in talks for a stake in Bain Capital's Bridge Data Centres, a Singapore based operator, with the size of the stake still being negotiated. The tailwind is AI driven data centre demand. The headwind is stretched valuations after a frantic year of deals. An advisor would say pension scale diversification is reasonable, but don't chase the same multiples personally.

blocks.title: Foreign Property Threshold Doubles, Insolvencies Stay High
blocks.script:
Start with the one that affects almost every cross-border or snowbird client file. Globe Advisor reports Budget 2026 proposes to raise the T1135 foreign property reporting threshold from $100,000 to $200,000, and the simplified-reporting ceiling from under $250,000 to under $500,000, for taxation years ending after 2026. That change alone would exempt approximately one-third of all current filers from the obligation to file, something like 240,000 taxpayers. It does not apply to this year's return, only tax years ending after 2026, so do not let clients skip their current T1135 on the strength of this headline.

Household stress is the backdrop. Wealth Professional's new data shows Canadian consumer insolvencies have stayed above 36,000 for a third straight quarter, the highest sustained pace since 2009, and that is landing right as holiday budgets climb and financial insecurity rises, especially among younger clients. If you have incorporated business owners or physicians in a life transition right now, divorce, retirement, practice sale, this is the moment to flag cash flow before they lever up for the season.

On fraud, deepfake attacks are climbing, hitting 44% of anti-fraud teams surveyed, with only a sliver rating their firm well prepared. Pair that with Capital One's finding that Canadians still trust banks over AI chatbots for money advice, and you have a good opening line with clients worried about scams: the trust gap is your selling point, use it.

The Quebecor-Telus story is already on your radar, but here is your angle: Telus's board warned the eighty-one-dollar bid would shrink dividends, citing 4.1 times leverage in the combined company. If you hold Telus for income in client portfolios, that yield compression risk needs a conversation now, not after a deal closes.

On the watch list today: the Bank of Canada's next rate decision lands December 9, its only remaining call of the year after October's quarter-point hike to 2.50%. Also smaller industry moves: BMO added six new ETFs, and Knowledge Bureau opened a new tax planning certificate for CFPs.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Throne Speech Tax Cuts, Record Wait Times, Prairie Health Risks
blocks.script:
The throne speech is the story your clients will be asking about today. Premier Wab Kinew delivered his fourth and final throne speech before next year's election, and the headline is a "mega-deduction" style middle-class tax cut coming in the spring budget. He didn't give you a number yet, but he framed it plainly: "the rich obviously have a lot of folks helping them, so we think it's the middle class's turn to get some help." For business clients, there's more: the province will match Ottawa's new federal tax deduction for business, and Manitoba has created a new chief mining officer role, filled by industry veteran Stacy Kennedy, aimed at cutting red tape for mining investment. On health, the government is promising the Victoria Hospital emergency room back open next summer, a second new ER in Eriksdale by next fall, free shingles vaccines for seniors 65 to 79 and immunocompromised adults starting in July, funding for police in schools, and new rules banning artificial intelligence generated images in real estate listings. The Opposition called it short on substance, and columnist Tom Brodbeck points out that reopening Victoria's ER won't fix the underlying wait time crunch.

That crunch is real and it's getting worse. A CBC analysis out today found Manitobans can wait nine months or longer for an ultrasound, fifteen months for a CT scan, and ten months for an MRI depending on where the scan gets sent, with one doctor calling the backlog worse than it has ever been. That is a talking point for any client with aging parents or chronic conditions, and it is pushing more Manitobans toward private cross-border imaging.

blocks.label: Parenting
blocks.title: Screen Time Surprise, and Less Paranoid Parenting
blocks.script:
An eight-year Finnish study followed children from the PANIC research project and found something unexpected: more accumulated screen time was linked to better cognitive processing by adolescence, not worse. Accumulating less unsupervised physical activity and more screen time from childhood to adolescence was associated with better cognition in adolescence, and the researchers say screen time can support cognitive processing. The catch is what children actually do on screens, coding or problem-solving appears to matter more than raw hours, and researchers stress this is association, not proof of causation.

Separately, a Globe and Mail essay this week pushes back against what the writer calls paranoid parenting, arguing kids need unsupervised freedom to build independence. For clients raising young families, it is a useful counterweight to headlines that treat every screen minute as damage.

blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Statement forensics, lesson 8: Goodwill and intangibles: what an impairment actually signals.

Kraft Heinz wrote down nine point three billion dollars of goodwill in one quarter back in 2019, tied to its Kraft and Oscar Mayer brands. The stock fell down over eight percent the next trading day. People read that as the business collapsing. It did not collapse. What collapsed was an accounting estimate made years earlier, when Kraft and Heinz merged and somebody priced the combined brand value too high.

Here is what goodwill actually is. When a company buys another company for more than the fair value of its identifiable assets, the excess sits on the balance sheet as goodwill. It is not cash, it is not a factory, it is the premium paid for reputation, customer relationships, expected synergies. Every year under United States accounting rules, management has to test whether that premium still holds up. If projected cash flows from that acquired business fall below what was assumed at purchase, they write it down. That write-down is the impairment.

The mistake people make is treating an impairment as new bad news about the future. It is not. It is a confession about the past, specifically about a price paid years ago that turned out to be wrong. The cash left the building at acquisition. The impairment changes earnings per share and book value, but it does not touch current cash flow. Check this on Thomson ONE in the cash flow statement: impairment charges get added back above the operating cash flow line, because they are non-cash.

What it does tell you, reliably, is that management's own forecast for that business segment has deteriorated enough to breach a threshold. That is useful. It is a lagging confirmation that a prior deal underperformed, and it can flag where a segment is struggling before the segment's own revenue line shows it clearly. What it cannot tell you is current competitive position, current demand, or whether the core business is healthy. For that you still need the revenue and margin trends underneath.

Always separate the impairment line from operating performance before you judge the quarter.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 37: Retirement income sequencing: which account to draw first and why.

The biggest mistake in retirement income planning is drawing RRSP or RRIF money last, because it feels like the one you're "saving." That instinct costs clients real dollars, and here's why.

Your accounts aren't equal. A Tax-Free Savings Account, or TFSA, grows and comes out with zero tax, ever. A non-registered account only gets taxed on the growth portion each year. An RRSP or RRIF, once you convert at 71, gets taxed at full marginal rate on every dollar withdrawn, and it also keeps growing, pushing future withdrawals into higher brackets and triggering Old Age Security clawback.

The general sequencing logic for 2026: spend non-registered investments first, because their tax drag is lowest and you want to preserve tax sheltered room elsewhere. Then draw some RRSP or RRIF, deliberately, even before you need the cash, to smooth your income across retirement rather than hitting a wall at 71. Save TFSA for last, because it's the only account that never triggers clawback and never triggers tax, so it's your most flexible buffer for large one-time needs or late-life top-ups.

Worked example. A retired Manitoba physician, age 62, has 900,000 dollars in a RRIF-eligible RRSP, 200,000 in non-registered investments, and 150,000 in a TFSA. If she spends TFSA first, by 71 her RRSP has kept compounding at say 5 percent, swelling past 1.3 million, forcing minimum withdrawals that push her into OAS clawback territory once she's 65 and collecting it. Instead, drawing 40,000 a year from the RRSP starting at 62, using lower brackets now while she has room, and topping up with non-registered funds, keeps her lifetime tax bill lower and her TFSA intact for flexibility at 80 or 85.

The one mistake: treating the RRSP as the account you touch last. It's usually the account you should start drawing from early, on purpose, before the government forces the pace with mandatory minimums.

Communication, lesson 37: Networking: introductions that people remember.

Harvard Business School researcher Alison Wood Brooks ran a study on conversations and found something specific: people remember the questions you asked them far more than the facts you told them about yourself. Her 2017 paper, published in Management Science, tracked speed daters and job interviewers. The people rated as most likeable asked, on average, nine more follow up questions per conversation than the least likeable ones. Not more questions overall. Follow up questions. The kind that prove you were listening to the last answer, not waiting for your turn.

Here is the mistake almost everyone makes at a networking event or board dinner: they lead with their own credential. "I'm an advisor, I work with founders on exits, I also sit on two nonprofit boards." That's a business card read aloud. Nobody remembers a business card. What they remember is the one moment you made them talk about something specific and then asked a second question about it.

Worked example. You meet someone at a board function who says, "I run operations for a mid-size logistics company." Weak move: "That's great, I work with a lot of operators too." Strong move: "What's the thing that broke this year that you didn't expect to?" They answer, say, "Our freight costs jumped 22 percent after a carrier consolidation, per the numbers our CFO showed the board in March." Now the follow up: "Did that change who you're negotiating contracts with, or just the price?" That second question is the one they'll bring up to their spouse that night, not your title.

The single mistake: treating the opener as the whole interaction instead of the first half of it. One good question with no follow up is just small talk with better phrasing.

An advisor says leadership changes rarely move your portfolio, stay diversified regardless of who sits in the chair.

Nvidia, the dominant AI chip maker, is in commentary today over culture, not silicon, with the Globe questioning strongman leadership patterns around founder control. The tailwind is its grip on AI hardware demand. The headwind is concentration risk tied to one personality. Wealth Professional's advisor panel confirms this changes how founders and investors think about every new share acquired, though eligibility requirements mean it won't apply to most business owners. For your incorporated clients who are planning a sale in five or ten years, this is worth a conversation now about share structure, because the exemption applies to individuals directly, not through a holding company.

CIRO told the Advocis symposium last week that a rule allowing securities-licensed advisors to incorporate is "some ways away", with the regulator's real goal being to build a model that's "evergreen" amid further developments.
